prompt: Let $X$ be a nonsingular matrix with columns $X_1,X_2,\dots,X_n$. Let $Y$ be the matrix with columns $X_2,X_3,\dots,X_n,0$. Show that the matrices $A=YX^{-1}$ and $B=X^{-1}Y$ have rank $n-1$ and have only $0$'s for eigenvalues.
answer: $Y=XJ$, where $J$ is the nilpotent shift matrix ($Je_j=e_{j+1}$, $Je_n=0$). So $B=J$ and $A=XJX^{-1}$ is similar to $J$, which has rank $n-1$ and only the eigenvalue $0$.

solutions.title: Write $Y$ as $X$ times a shift
solutions.body:
Let $e_1,\dots,e_n$ be the standard basis and let $J$ be the $n\times n$ matrix with $Je_j=e_{j+1}$ for $j<n$ and $Je_n=0$. So $J$ has ones just below the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. The $j$-th column of $XJ$ is $XJe_j$. For $j<n$ this is $Xe_{j+1}=X_{j+1}$, and for $j=n$ it is $0$. Hence $XJ=Y$, and
$$B=X^{-1}Y=J,\qquad A=YX^{-1}=XJX^{-1}.$$
The columns of $J$ are $e_2,\dots,e_n,0$, so $\operatorname{rank}J=n-1$. Also $J^n=0$ (each power shifts further down), so every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $J$ satisfies $\lambda^n=0$, i.e. $\lambda=0$. Since $J$ is strictly lower triangular, its characteristic polynomial is $x^n$. Rank and eigenvalues are invariant under similarity, so $A=XJX^{-1}$ and $B=J$ both have rank $n-1$ and only the eigenvalue $0$. ∎

prompt:
Let $f$ be a continuous function on $[0,1]$ such that for every $x\in[0,1]$ we have $\displaystyle\int_x^1 f(t)\,dt\ge\frac{1-x^2}{2}$. Show that
$$\int_0^1 f^2(t)\,dt\ge\frac13 .$$
answer: Integrate the hypothesis over $x\in[0,1]$ and swap the order: $\int_0^1 tf(t)\,dt\ge\frac13$. Then $0\le\int_0^1(f-x)^2$ (or Cauchy–Schwarz) gives $\int f^2\ge2\int xf-\frac13\ge\frac13$.

solutions.title: Fubini, then expand a square
solutions.body:
Integrate the hypothesis over $x\in[0,1]$ and exchange the order of integration (Fubini, $f$ is continuous):
$$\int_0^1 t f(t)\,dt=\int_0^1\int_0^t f(t)\,dx\,dt=\int_0^1\int_x^1f(t)\,dt\,dx\ge\int_0^1\frac{1-x^2}{2}\,dx=\frac12\Big(1-\frac13\Big)=\frac13 .$$
Now
$$0\le\int_0^1\big(f(x)-x\big)^2dx=\int_0^1f^2-2\int_0^1xf(x)\,dx+\frac13,$$
so
$$\int_0^1f^2\ge2\int_0^1xf(x)\,dx-\frac13\ge\frac23-\frac13=\frac13 .$$
Equality holds for $f(x)=x$. ∎

solutions.title: Cauchy–Schwarz
solutions.body:
As in the first solution, $\int_0^1tf(t)\,dt\ge\frac13$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,
$$\frac13\le\int_0^1t\,f(t)\,dt\le\Big(\int_0^1t^2dt\Big)^{1/2}\Big(\int_0^1f^2\Big)^{1/2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\Big(\int_0^1f^2\Big)^{1/2}.$$
Squaring gives $\frac19\le\frac13\int_0^1f^2$, i.e. $\int_0^1f^2\ge\frac13$. ∎

prompt:
Let $f$ be twice continuously differentiable on $(0,+\infty)$ such that $\lim\limits_{x\to0+}f'(x)=-\infty$ and $\lim\limits_{x\to0+}f''(x)=+\infty$. Show that
$$\lim_{x\to0+}\frac{f(x)}{f'(x)}=0 .$$
answer: Near $0$, $f'<0$ is increasing, so for $0<x<x_0$: $0<f(x)-f(x_0)\le(x_0-x)|f'(x)|$. Dividing by $f'(x)\to-\infty$ gives $-x_0\le\liminf\frac{f}{f'}\le\limsup\frac{f}{f'}\le0$; then let $x_0\to0$.

solutions.title: Mean value estimate near $0$
solutions.body:
Choose $r>0$ with $f'(x)<0$ and $f''(x)>0$ on $(0,r)$. Then $f$ is decreasing and $f'$ is increasing on $(0,r)$. Fix $x_0\in(0,r)$ and let $0<x<x_0$. For $t\in[x,x_0]$ we have $f'(x)\le f'(t)<0$, i.e. $|f'(t)|\le|f'(x)|$. Hence
$$0<f(x)-f(x_0)=\int_x^{x_0}|f'(t)|\,dt\le(x_0-x)\,|f'(x)| .$$
Divide by $f'(x)=-|f'(x)|<0$:
$$-(x_0-x)\le\frac{f(x)}{f'(x)}-\frac{f(x_0)}{f'(x)}<0 .$$
As $x\to0+$, $f'(x)\to-\infty$ while $f(x_0)$ is fixed, so $\frac{f(x_0)}{f'(x)}\to0$. Therefore
$$-x_0\le\liminf_{x\to0+}\frac{f(x)}{f'(x)}\le\limsup_{x\to0+}\frac{f(x)}{f'(x)}\le0 .$$
This holds for every $x_0\in(0,r)$. Letting $x_0\to0$ shows that the limit exists and equals $0$. ∎

prompt:
Let $F:(1,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be the function defined by
$$F(x)=\int_x^{x^2}\frac{dt}{\ln t}.$$
Show that $F$ is one-to-one (i.e. injective) and find the range (i.e. set of values) of $F$.
answer: $F'(x)=\frac{x-1}{\ln x}>0$, so $F$ is strictly increasing. With $t=e^v$, $F(x)=\int_{\ln x}^{2\ln x}\frac{e^v}{v}dv$ lies strictly between $x\ln2$ and $x^2\ln2$. The range is $(\ln2,\infty)$.

solutions.title: Derivative and a two-sided bound
solutions.body:
**Injectivity.** By the fundamental theorem of calculus and the chain rule,
$$F'(x)=\frac{2x}{\ln(x^2)}-\frac{1}{\ln x}=\frac{x}{\ln x}-\frac1{\ln x}=\frac{x-1}{\ln x}>0\qquad(x>1).$$
So $F$ is continuous and strictly increasing on $(1,\infty)$, hence one-to-one.

**Range.** Substitute $t=e^v$, $dt=e^v\,dv$:
$$F(x)=\int_{\ln x}^{2\ln x}\frac{e^v}{v}\,dv .$$
On the interval of integration $x=e^{\ln x}\le e^v\le e^{2\ln x}=x^2$, with strict inequality except at the endpoints. Also $\int_{\ln x}^{2\ln x}\frac{dv}{v}=\ln2$. Hence
$$x\ln2<F(x)<x^2\ln2\qquad(x>1).$$
Letting $x\to1+$ gives $\lim_{x\to1+}F(x)=\ln2$, and $F(x)>x\ln2\to\infty$ as $x\to\infty$. Since $F$ is continuous and strictly increasing, its range is the open interval between these two limits:
$$F\big((1,\infty)\big)=(\ln2,\infty) .$$

**Answer: the range is $(\ln 2,\infty)$.** ∎

prompt:
Let $A$ and $B$ be real $n\times n$ matrices. Assume that there exist $n+1$ different real numbers $t_1,t_2,\dots,t_{n+1}$ such that the matrices
$$C_i=A+t_iB,\qquad i=1,2,\dots,n+1,$$
are nilpotent (i.e. $C_i^n=0$). Show that both $A$ and $B$ are nilpotent.
answer: $(A+tB)^n=A^n+tP_1+\dots+t^{n-1}P_{n-1}+t^nB^n$. Each entry is a polynomial in $t$ of degree $\le n$ with $n+1$ roots, so it is identically zero. In particular $A^n=B^n=0$.

solutions.title: Polynomial in $t$ with too many roots
solutions.body:
Expanding the product $(A+tB)^n$ (the matrices need not commute, but the expansion is still a polynomial in the scalar $t$) gives
$$(A+tB)^n=A^n+tP_1+t^2P_2+\dots+t^{n-1}P_{n-1}+t^nB^n$$
for some matrices $P_1,\dots,P_{n-1}$ that do not depend on $t$. Fix an entry position $(i,j)$ and let $a,p_1,\dots,p_{n-1},b$ be the $(i,j)$ entries of $A^n,P_1,\dots,P_{n-1},B^n$. The polynomial
$$p(t)=a+p_1t+\dots+p_{n-1}t^{n-1}+bt^n$$
has degree at most $n$ and vanishes at the $n+1$ distinct points $t_1,\dots,t_{n+1}$, because $(A+t_kB)^n=0$. Hence $p$ is the zero polynomial, and in particular $a=0$ and $b=0$. This holds for every position $(i,j)$, so $A^n=0$ and $B^n=0$: both $A$ and $B$ are nilpotent. ∎

prompt:
Let $p>1$. Show that there exists a constant $K_p>0$ such that for every $x,y\in\mathbb R$ satisfying $|x|^p+|y|^p=2$ we have
$$(x-y)^2\le K_p\big(4-(x+y)^2\big).$$
answer: The denominator $4-(x+y)^2$ vanishes on the curve only at $(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1)$ (strict power-mean inequality), so compactness handles everything away from these points. Near $(1,1)$, Taylor's formula for $t^p$ gives $2\ge2s^p+md^2$ with $s=\frac{x+y}2$, $d=\frac{x-y}2$, hence $1-s\ge\frac{m}{2p}d^2$.

solutions.title: Compactness away from $(\pm1,\pm1)$, Taylor near them
solutions.body:
Let $\Gamma=\{(x,y):|x|^p+|y|^p=2\}$, a compact curve. Write $s=\frac{x+y}2$ and $d=\frac{x-y}2$. The inequality reads $4d^2\le4K_p(1-s^2)$.

**Step 1: where the right side vanishes.** The function $t\mapsto t^p$ is strictly convex on $[0,\infty)$, so for $(x,y)\in\Gamma$
$$|s|\le\frac{|x|+|y|}2\le\Big(\frac{|x|^p+|y|^p}{2}\Big)^{1/p}=1,$$
with equality in the second step only if $|x|=|y|$. Equality in the first step needs $x,y$ of the same sign. So $1-s^2=0$ on $\Gamma$ only at $(1,1)$ and $(-1,-1)$. Also $|x-y|\le|x|+|y|\le2$ on $\Gamma$, so $(x-y)^2\le4$.

**Step 2: near $(1,1)$.** Let $U=\{(x,y)\in\Gamma:\tfrac12<x<\tfrac32,\ \tfrac12<y<\tfrac32\}$ and $m=p(p-1)\min_{t\in[1/2,3/2]}t^{p-2}>0$. For $(x,y)\in U$, the numbers $s$, $x=s+d$ and $y=s-d$ all lie in $(\tfrac12,\tfrac32)$. Taylor's formula for $\varphi(t)=t^p$ at $s$ gives
$$x^p+y^p=\varphi(s+d)+\varphi(s-d)=2\varphi(s)+\tfrac12\big(\varphi''(\xi_1)+\varphi''(\xi_2)\big)d^2\ge2s^p+md^2,$$
with $\xi_1,\xi_2\in(\tfrac12,\tfrac32)$. Since $x^p+y^p=2$, we get $s^p\le1-u$ with $u=\frac m2d^2\in[0,1]$. Because $t\mapsto t^{1/p}$ is concave, $(1-u)^{1/p}\le1-\frac up$. Hence
$$1-s\ge\frac{m}{2p}d^2,\qquad 1-s^2=(1-s)(1+s)\ge1-s\ge\frac{m}{2p}d^2,$$
so $(x-y)^2=4d^2\le\frac{2p}{m}\big(4-(x+y)^2\big)$ on $U$. The substitution $(x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y)$ preserves $\Gamma$ and both sides of the inequality, so the same bound holds on $-U$, a neighbourhood of $(-1,-1)$.

**Step 3: the rest.** $R=\Gamma\setminus(U\cup-U)$ is compact (it is closed in $\Gamma$, since $U$ and $-U$ are relatively open) and contains neither $(1,1)$ nor $(-1,-1)$. By Step 1 the continuous function $4-(x+y)^2$ is positive on $R$, so it has a positive minimum $\delta$ there. Then on $R$, $(x-y)^2\le4\le\frac4\delta\big(4-(x+y)^2\big)$.

So $K_p=\max\big(\frac{2p}{m},\frac4\delta\big)$ works on all of $\Gamma$. ∎

*Remark.* Near $(1,1)$ the sharp local ratio is $\frac{1}{p-1}$: putting $x=1+t$ one finds $(x-y)^2\approx4t^2$ and $4-(x+y)^2\approx4(p-1)t^2$. This shows why $p>1$ is needed.

solutions.title: Test vectors, then compare components
solutions.body:
Write $A=(a_{ij})$. The hypothesis is $u^{\mathsf T}Au=0$ for all $u$.

**a)** With $u=e_k$: $a_{kk}=e_k^{\mathsf T}Ae_k=0$. With $u=e_k+e_m$ ($k\ne m$):
$$0=(e_k+e_m)^{\mathsf T}A(e_k+e_m)=a_{kk}+a_{km}+a_{mk}+a_{mm}=a_{km}+a_{mk}.$$
So $a_{mk}=-a_{km}$ for all $k,m$, i.e. $A^{\mathsf T}=-A$.

**b)** By a),
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&a_{12}&a_{13}\\-a_{12}&0&a_{23}\\-a_{13}&-a_{23}&0\end{pmatrix}.$$
Put $v=(v_1,v_2,v_3)=(-a_{23},\,a_{13},\,-a_{12})$. For $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)^{\mathsf T}$,
$$v\times u=\begin{pmatrix}v_2u_3-v_3u_2\\v_3u_1-v_1u_3\\v_1u_2-v_2u_1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}a_{12}u_2+a_{13}u_3\\-a_{12}u_1+a_{23}u_3\\-a_{13}u_1-a_{23}u_2\end{pmatrix}=Au .$$
∎

prompt:
Let $\{b_n\}_{n=0}^\infty$ be a sequence of positive real numbers such that $b_0=1$ and
$$b_n=2+\sqrt{b_{n-1}}-2\sqrt{1+\sqrt{b_{n-1}}}.$$
Calculate
$$\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n2^n .$$

solutions.title: Substitute $a_n=1+\sqrt{b_n}$ and telescope
solutions.body:
Let $a_n=1+\sqrt{b_n}$, so $a_0=2$ and $a_n\ge1$. The recurrence says
$$b_n=1+a_{n-1}-2\sqrt{a_{n-1}}=\big(\sqrt{a_{n-1}}-1\big)^2 .$$
Since $\sqrt{a_{n-1}}\ge1$, this gives $\sqrt{b_n}=\sqrt{a_{n-1}}-1$, i.e. $a_n=\sqrt{a_{n-1}}$. Hence $a_n=2^{2^{-n}}$, and $b_n=(a_n-1)^2$. Using $a_n^2=a_{n-1}$,
$$b_n2^n=(a_n^2-2a_n+1)2^n=(a_{n-1}-1)2^n-(a_n-1)2^{n+1}.$$
The sum telescopes:
$$\sum_{n=1}^Nb_n2^n=(a_0-1)\cdot2-(a_N-1)2^{N+1}=2-2\cdot\frac{2^{2^{-N}}-1}{2^{-N}} .$$
With $x=2^{-N}\to0$ and $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{2^x-1}{x}=\ln2$ (the derivative of $2^x$ at $0$),
$$\sum_{n=1}^\infty b_n2^n=2-2\ln2\approx0.6137 .$$

**Answer: $2-2\ln2$.**

prompt:
Let all roots of an $n$-th degree polynomial $P(z)$ with complex coefficients lie on the unit circle in the complex plane. Prove that all roots of the polynomial
$$2zP'(z)-nP(z)$$
lie on the same circle.
answer: For $P(z)\ne0$: $\dfrac{2zP'(z)-nP(z)}{P(z)}=\sum_k\dfrac{z+\alpha_k}{z-\alpha_k}$, whose real part is $\sum_k\dfrac{|z|^2-1}{|z-\alpha_k|^2}$. This is non-zero when $|z|\ne1$.

solutions.title: Logarithmic derivative and real parts
solutions.body:
We may assume $P$ is monic, $P(z)=\prod_{k=1}^n(z-\alpha_k)$ with $|\alpha_k|=1$ (repetitions allowed). Let $Q(z)=2zP'(z)-nP(z)$. Its leading coefficient is $2n-n=n\ne0$, so $Q$ has degree $n$.

Let $Q(z)=0$. If $P(z)=0$, then $z$ is some $\alpha_k$ and $|z|=1$. Otherwise, since $\frac{P'}{P}=\sum_k\frac1{z-\alpha_k}$,
$$0=\frac{Q(z)}{P(z)}=\sum_{k=1}^n\Big(\frac{2z}{z-\alpha_k}-1\Big)=\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{z+\alpha_k}{z-\alpha_k}.$$
For any $z\ne\alpha$,
$$\frac{z+\alpha}{z-\alpha}=\frac{(z+\alpha)(\bar z-\bar\alpha)}{|z-\alpha|^2}=\frac{|z|^2-|\alpha|^2+(\alpha\bar z-z\bar\alpha)}{|z-\alpha|^2},$$
and $\alpha\bar z-z\bar\alpha$ is purely imaginary. Taking real parts,
$$0=\operatorname{Re}\frac{Q(z)}{P(z)}=\big(|z|^2-1\big)\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{1}{|z-\alpha_k|^2}.$$
The sum is positive, so $|z|=1$. Hence all roots of $Q$ lie on the unit circle. ∎

prompt:
a) Prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a positive integer $n$ and real numbers $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ such that
$$\max_{x\in[-1,1]}\Big|x-\sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_kx^{2k+1}\Big|<\varepsilon .$$

b) Prove that for every odd continuous function $f$ on $[-1,1]$ and for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a positive integer $n$ and real numbers $\mu_1,\dots,\mu_n$ such that
$$\max_{x\in[-1,1]}\Big|f(x)-\sum_{k=1}^n\mu_kx^{2k+1}\Big|<\varepsilon .$$
(Recall that $f$ is odd means that $f(x)=-f(-x)$ for all $x\in[-1,1]$.)
answer: a) $x-\sum_{k=1}^n(-1)^{k+1}\binom nk x^{2k+1}=x(1-x^2)^n$, which is uniformly small for large $n$. b) Weierstrass gives an odd polynomial $q$ close to $f$; replace its linear term $b_0x$ using a).

solutions.title: Binomial expansion and Weierstrass
solutions.body:
**a)** We may assume $0<\varepsilon<1$. Choose $n$ with $(1-\varepsilon^2)^n<\varepsilon$ and let $\lambda_k=(-1)^{k+1}\binom nk$. Then
$$x-\sum_{k=1}^n\lambda_kx^{2k+1}=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nkx^{2k+1}=x(1-x^2)^n .$$
For $|x|<\varepsilon$: $|x(1-x^2)^n|\le|x|<\varepsilon$. For $\varepsilon\le|x|\le1$: $|x(1-x^2)^n|\le(1-\varepsilon^2)^n<\varepsilon$. So the maximum, which is attained on the compact interval, is $<\varepsilon$.

**b)** By the Weierstrass approximation theorem there is a polynomial $p$ with $|f-p|<\varepsilon/2$ on $[-1,1]$. Its odd part $q(x)=\frac12\big(p(x)-p(-x)\big)$ satisfies, because $f$ is odd,
$$f(x)-q(x)=\tfrac12\big(f(x)-p(x)\big)-\tfrac12\big(f(-x)-p(-x)\big),\qquad\text{so}\quad\max_{|x|\le1}|f-q|<\frac\varepsilon2 .$$
Write $q(x)=b_0x+\sum_{k=1}^mb_kx^{2k+1}$. If $b_0=0$ we are done. Otherwise apply a) with $\frac{\varepsilon}{2|b_0|}$: there are $n$ and $\lambda_k$ with $\big|b_0x-\sum_{k=1}^nb_0\lambda_kx^{2k+1}\big|<\frac\varepsilon2$ on $[-1,1]$. Then
$$\sum_{k=1}^{\max(m,n)}\mu_kx^{2k+1},\qquad\mu_k=b_k+b_0\lambda_k$$
(with $b_k=0$ for $k>m$ and $\lambda_k=0$ for $k>n$) differs from $f$ by less than $\frac\varepsilon2+\frac\varepsilon2=\varepsilon$ on $[-1,1]$. ∎

prompt:
a) Prove that every function of the form
$$f(x)=\frac{a_0}{2}+\cos x+\sum_{n=2}^Na_n\cos(nx)$$
with $|a_0|<1$ has positive as well as negative values in the period $[0,2\pi)$.

b) Prove that the function
$$F(x)=\sum_{n=1}^{100}\cos\big(n^{3/2}x\big)$$
has at least $40$ zeros in the interval $(0,1000)$.
answer: a) $\int_0^{2\pi}f(x)(1\pm\cos x)\,dx=\pi(a_0\pm1)$. b) If $F$ kept one sign on an interval $(y,y+h)$, then $\left|\int F\cos x\right|\le\left|\int F\right|$. But $\left|\int F\right|<6$, while $\left|\int F\cos x\right|>\frac h2-6$. So $F$ changes sign on every interval of length $24$, and $(0,1000)$ contains $41$ disjoint such intervals.

solutions.title: Test against $1\pm\cos x$, then integrate against $\cos x$
solutions.body:
**a)** By orthogonality of $1,\cos x,\cos2x,\dots$ on $[0,2\pi]$,
$$\int_0^{2\pi}f(x)(1\pm\cos x)\,dx=\frac{a_0}{2}\cdot2\pi\pm\int_0^{2\pi}\cos^2x\,dx=\pi(a_0\pm1).$$
If $f\ge0$ everywhere, then, since $1-\cos x\ge0$, $\pi(a_0-1)\ge0$, i.e. $a_0\ge1$. If $f\le0$ everywhere, then $\pi(a_0+1)\le0$, i.e. $a_0\le-1$. Both contradict $|a_0|<1$. So $f$ takes a negative value and a positive value.

**b)** We show that for every $N$, every $y\in\mathbb R$ and every $h\ge24$, the function $F_N(x)=\sum_{n=1}^N\cos(n^{3/2}x)$ takes both positive and negative values on $(y,y+h)$. Let
$$I_1=\int_y^{y+h}F_N(x)\,dx,\qquad I_2=\int_y^{y+h}F_N(x)\cos x\,dx .$$
If $F_N$ had constant sign on the interval, then $|I_2|\le\int|F_N|=|I_1|$. So it suffices to prove $|I_2|>|I_1|$. We use $\big|\int_y^{y+h}\cos(\alpha x)\,dx\big|\le\frac2{|\alpha|}$ for $\alpha\ne0$.

*Bound for $I_1$:*
$$|I_1|\le\sum_{n=1}^N\frac{2}{n^{3/2}}<2\Big(1+\int_1^\infty t^{-3/2}dt\Big)=6 .$$

*Bound for $I_2$:* Since $\cos x\cos(\beta x)=\frac12\big(\cos((\beta-1)x)+\cos((\beta+1)x)\big)$,
$$I_2=\frac12\int_y^{y+h}(1+\cos2x)\,dx+\frac12\sum_{n=2}^N\int_y^{y+h}\Big(\cos\big((n^{3/2}-1)x\big)+\cos\big((n^{3/2}+1)x\big)\Big)dx=\frac h2+\Delta,$$
where
$$|\Delta|\le\frac12+\sum_{n=2}^N\frac{2}{n^{3/2}-1}\le\frac12+\frac{2}{2\sqrt2-1}+3\sum_{n\ge3}n^{-3/2}.$$
Here we used $n^{3/2}-1\ge\frac23n^{3/2}$ for $n\ge3$. Now $\frac2{2\sqrt2-1}<1.1$ and $3\sum_{n\ge3}n^{-3/2}\le3\int_2^\infty t^{-3/2}dt=3\sqrt2<4.25$, so $|\Delta|<5.85<6$. Hence $|I_2|>\frac h2-6\ge6>|I_1|$ for $h\ge24$.

So $F=F_{100}$ takes both signs, and by the intermediate value theorem has a zero, in each of the $41$ disjoint intervals $(24j,24j+24)$, $j=0,1,\dots,40$, all contained in $(0,1000)$ since $41\cdot24=984$. Thus $F$ has at least $41\ge40$ zeros in $(0,1000)$. ∎

prompt:
Suppose that $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^\infty$ is a sequence of continuous functions on the interval $[0,1]$ such that
$$\int_0^1f_m(x)f_n(x)\,dx=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }n=m\\0&\text{if }n\ne m\end{cases}$$
and
$$\sup\{|f_n(x)|:x\in[0,1]\text{ and }n=1,2,\dots\}<+\infty .$$
Show that there exists no subsequence $\{f_{n_k}\}$ of $\{f_n\}$ such that $\lim\limits_{k\to\infty}f_{n_k}(x)$ exists for all $x\in[0,1]$.
answer: If $f_{n_k}\to f$ pointwise, dominated convergence (the functions are uniformly bounded) gives $\int(f_{n_k}-f_{n_{k+1}})^2\to0$. But by orthonormality this integral equals $2$ for every $k$.

solutions.title: Dominated convergence against orthonormality
solutions.body:
Let $M$ be the uniform bound, and suppose $f_{n_k}(x)\to f(x)$ for every $x\in[0,1]$, with $n_1<n_2<\cdots$. Then $g_k=f_{n_k}-f_{n_{k+1}}\to0$ pointwise and $|g_k|\le2M$. So $g_k^2\to0$ pointwise with $g_k^2\le4M^2$, which is integrable on $[0,1]$. By Lebesgue's dominated convergence theorem, $\int_0^1g_k^2\to0$. But since $n_k\ne n_{k+1}$, orthonormality gives for every $k$
$$\int_0^1g_k^2=\int_0^1f_{n_k}^2-2\int_0^1f_{n_k}f_{n_{k+1}}+\int_0^1f_{n_{k+1}}^2=1-0+1=2 .$$
This is a contradiction. ∎

solutions.title: Bessel's inequality
solutions.body:
Suppose $f_{n_k}\to f$ pointwise. Then $f$ is measurable with $|f|\le M$, so $f\in L^2[0,1]$. By dominated convergence (dominating functions $M^2$ and $M|f|\le M^2$),
$$\int_0^1f_{n_k}^2\to\int_0^1f^2\qquad\text{and}\qquad\int_0^1f\,f_{n_k}\to\int_0^1f^2 .$$
The first limit gives $\int_0^1f^2=1$. On the other hand, by Bessel's inequality for the orthonormal system $(f_n)$,
$$\sum_n\Big(\int_0^1f\,f_n\Big)^2\le\int_0^1f^2<\infty,$$
so $\int_0^1f\,f_n\to0$ as $n\to\infty$, and in particular along $n_k$. Hence $\int_0^1f^2=0$, contradicting $\int_0^1f^2=1$. ∎
